To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effects of NMDA receptor antagonist drugs on prepulse inhibition of the acoustic starttle reflex and on prepulse- elicited reactivity in C57BL/6 mice are not identical to those of the dopamine receptor agonist drug apomorphine.
the effects on prepulse reactivity in the PPI paradigm of dizocilpine and phencyclidines were opposite to the effects of apomorphine.
both drugs exhibited tendency to attenuate PPI and prepulse-elicitation at higher doses when prepulse-elicitability was severely disrupted.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of dizocilpine and phencyclidines on PPI and prepulse-elicitable reactivity in C57BL/6J mice.
the possible effects of NMDA receptor blockade on PPI and on prepulse-activated reactivity.
the development and evaluation of the PPI model as a potential screening tool for the detection of atypical antipsychotic drugs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NMDA antagonists do not enhance the prepulse-eliciting reaction, and therefore they do not affect the PPI of the acoustic startler response in the same way that the dopamine agonists do.
NMDA antagonists and dopamine receptor agonists have differential effects on the startle response and on the PPI of the startle response.

PPI disruption by noncompetitive N-Methyl-D-Aspartic Acid receptor (NMDAR) antagonists can be differentiated from apomorphines-induced PPI disruption via their concomitant effect on prepulse- elicited reactivity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PPI disruption by NMDA receptor blockade is not associated with a reduction in prepulse-elicitable reactivity, and that PPI disruption is not a reliable index of prepulse-elicitated reactivity.
NMDA antagonists disrupt PII via interference with a pathway that is not sensitive to apomorphines, whereas apomorphines disrupt PII via an interference with a pathway sensitive to NMDA antagonism.
PPI disruption by NMDA receptor antagonist is associated with a decrease in prepulse-eliciting reactivity, whereas that by apomorphine is associated with an increase in prepulse- elicited reactivity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prepulse-eliciting reactivity is a sensitive indicator of changes in the neural systems underlying the PPI response.
PPI is a more complex phenomenon than previously thought, and that the effects of a drug may depend on the degree to which PPI is disrupted.
the PPI of the acoustic start reflex paradigm may be a useful tool in the study of schizophrenia.
